lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on how regulators went wrong
lead.head: Lawmaker, cop and judge in one

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 99

body: Economists, Amit Varma said, are usu­ally the bringers of bad news. This episode came sand­wiched be­tween two pieces of good news. In the mid­dle was a story Varma called “scary”: how India’s reg­u­la­tors came to hold the pow­ers of a par­lia­ment, a po­lice force and a court[[x1]].

Varma began with first prin­ci­ples. In the lib­eral con­cep­tion, we give the state a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence, sur­ren­der­ing some of our rights so that it can pro­tect the rest through the rule of law.
Once that rule of law is in place, he ar­gued, mar­kets work beau­ti­fully. “In a mar­ket­place which is func­tion­ing well,” he said, “com­pe­ti­tion is the best reg­u­la­tion.” {099-C01}
Then Ajay Shah, whom Varma in­tro­duced as the India ex­pert on the sub­ject, took over.
## By de­sign

Since the 17th cen­tury, Shah said, lib­eral democ­racy has worked by dis­pers­ing power. The leg­is­la­ture writes the law, the ex­ec­u­tive in­ves­ti­gates and pros­e­cutes, and only a judge may pun­ish.

Regulators break that rule on pur­pose. Parliament gives a spe­cialised agency a nar­row power to write rules, and the same team po­lices and pros­e­cutes. “So it’s like the po­lice and the par­lia­ment have been fused into one agency,” Shah said. {099-C11}
The bar­gain works only if the del­e­ga­tion is sur­gi­cal, he said: one nar­row power for one mar­ket fail­ure.
## What India did

Indian reg­u­la­tors such as RBI and SEBI went fur­ther. They took the ju­di­cial power to pun­ish too, amid low lev­els of rule of law. “Suddenly you now have a mon­ster of 17th cen­tury po­lit­i­cal phi­los­o­phy,” Shah said.
The peo­ple who built these agen­cies were his friends, he said, and they meant well. They sim­ply lacked the knowl­edge.

The re­sult, he ar­gued, is that the 1991 re­forms did not end cen­tral plan­ning. Something like 75 per cent of the econ­omy came under reg­u­la­tors, whose staff con­trol prod­ucts and pro­cesses in more in­tru­sive de­tail than the old, dis­tant state ever did. {099-C13}
Firms whose sur­vival de­pends on the reg­u­la­tor stop speak­ing. “You get a si­lence of the grave­yard in the pub­lic do­main,” Shah said. With it go com­pe­ti­tion, entry and in­no­va­tion.
Varma needed a chap­ter break to re­cover. “Power cor­rupts, ab­so­lute power cor­rupts ab­so­lutely,” he said.
## The way back

The fix, Shah said, lies in the laws that cre­ate reg­u­la­tors: nar­row each del­e­ga­tion of law-making power, wrap rule-making and li­cens­ing in due process with a right of ap­peal, and send pros­e­cu­tions to the High Courts. {#fixit}

Much of that think­ing is al­ready in the draft law of the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission, whose tech­ni­cal team Shah co-led. It has not been en­acted, but “the jour­ney of progress is a story of in­tel­lec­tual per­sua­sion,” he said.

Hence the sec­ond piece of good news. The bank­ruptcy reg­u­la­tor IBBI had adopted a reg­u­la­tion on how it makes reg­u­la­tions, and later SEBI did the same. On the morn­ing of record­ing, Shah got an SMS that RBI had fol­lowed. {099-S06}

“At this point, I think the in­tel­lec­tual ar­gu­ment has been won,” he said. It is not the end of the jour­ney: a regulator’s board bind­ing its own staff is weaker than Parliament bind­ing the agency.
Varma of­fered a fist bump, and an image: “One baby step at a time, the in­fant crawls away from the precipice, but it can still hear the laboured breath­ing of the mon­ster.”

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Five Star in the ATM

body: Many years ago, Ajay Shah said, a bank wanted to coax cus­tomers away from branch coun­ters and to­wards ATMs. Its idea was to stock Cadbury Five Star bars in­side the ma­chines, so that a with­drawal of more than Rs 5,000 would also bring a choco­late. {099-S02}
Sad story num­ber one, Shah said: the bank had to seek the regulator’s ap­proval. Sad story num­ber two: it was de­nied. Candy along with cash, the reg­u­la­tor said, was undig­ni­fied.

Shah al­lowed that it may not work this way today. But the regulator’s at­ti­tude, as he de­scribed it, was sim­ple: ev­ery­thing is banned until ap­proved. “I will not allow you to launch a prod­uct until I ap­prove the prod­uct.” {#approve}

third.head: Zero, now imported

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the trade deal with the UK

body: Closing the hosts’ sec­ond episode on glob­al­i­sa­tion, Ajay Shah pre­dicted good things for India’s trade pol­icy, going only by news­pa­pers and “un­der­stand­ing the chess­board”. The first piece has ar­rived: a free trade agree­ment with the UK[[x2]].

Going by news re­ports, which he warned are no sub­sti­tute for the legal text, tar­iffs fall on 90 per cent of prod­ucts along a ten-year glide path, reach­ing zero for 80 per cent. {#eighty} Certainty, he said, forces firms to raise pro­duc­tiv­ity or go out of busi­ness.

British com­pa­nies will also be able to bid in Indian gov­ern­ment pro­cure­ment. “Once you’ve got zero tar­iff with one coun­try,” he asked, “what’s the point of hav­ing tar­iffs with any­body else?” {099-S01}
Amit Varma pitched a block­buster called *Return to Zero*: India in­vented zero, and now the for­eign­ers were bring­ing it back. {099-J02}

box.title: The code that wasn’t enacted
box.text: The Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission left two vol­umes. The first, Ajay Shah said, is a crisp sum­mary of 20 years of Indian re­search on reg­u­la­tory the­ory; the sec­ond, the draft Indian Financial Code[[x8]][[x9]], is a role model for draft­ing laws. {#volumeone}

sections.label: The theory
sections.head: A rupee here, a fortune there
sections.caption: the theory and history of regulation
body: Amit Varma began with a pot­ted his­tory of ideas. Economists first ex­plained bad reg­u­la­tion with cap­ture the­ory, in which lob­bies seize the reg­u­la­tory process. Then George Stigler’s fa­mous 1971 essay, *The Theory of Economic Regulation*, set out three ax­ioms: the state has co­er­cive power, a pri­vate party that gets it used on its be­half ben­e­fits, so every pri­vate party has a ra­tio­nal self-interest in try­ing. {099-R03}

Public choice the­ory ex­plains why the lob­bies win: con­cen­trated ben­e­fits and dif­fuse costs[[x10]]. A tax that takes one rupee a year from every cit­i­zen goes un­no­ticed, while the com­pany be­hind it col­lects a for­tune and is happy to give 30 per cent of it to MPs and cor­po­ra­tors. {#thirtypercent}
“Every reg­u­la­tion harms the peo­ple,” Varma said, but the cost is so small and so in­vis­i­ble that no­body protests. {099-C05}
## Strange bed­fel­lows

In Bruce Yandle’s *Bootleggers and Baptists*, the preacher who cam­paigns for pro­hi­bi­tion finds an ally in the boot­leg­ger who prof­its from it. {099-C07} Varma’s mod­ern cases: to­bacco com­pa­nies back­ing FDA pre-approval for new cig­a­rettes, and the sugar lobby fund­ing stud­ies that blamed fat.

~ Then there is the in­ter­ven­tion­ist spi­ral that Hayek and Mises warned of. Rent con­trols bring hous­ing short­ages, short­ages bring sub­si­dies, then zon­ing laws, until ev­ery­thing “starts to go to hell”. {099-C09}

quote.text: We talk about mar­ket fail­ure, but mar­ket fail­ure is rare. Government fail­ure is ubiq­ui­tous.

sections.label: Why a regulator?
sections.head: The surgical bargain
sections.caption: why anyone sets up a regulator
body: Why set up a reg­u­la­tor, when a gov­ern­ment de­part­ment can co­erce firms too? In the early 1990s, Ajay Shah said, the hope was that reg­u­la­tors would bring a mod­ern, mar­ket-minded cul­ture. “Okay, I hate to break your bub­ble. It didn’t hap­pen at all.” {#bubble}

Regulatory the­ory of­fers two bet­ter rea­sons. One is spe­cial­i­sa­tion. Government de­part­ments move peo­ple every five years, al­most at ran­dom. Shah would like staff to ro­tate be­tween reg­u­la­tors; India’s cra­dle-to-grave em­ploy­ment in one agency is, he said, “a very bad idea”. {#rotation}
## A de­lib­er­ate breach

The other rea­son is a de­lib­er­ate breach of the sep­a­ra­tion of pow­ers[[x11]]: fus­ing the power to write law with the power to en­force it. The world’s most fa­mous ex­am­ple, the US Securities and Exchange Commission, came up in the 1930s dur­ing the Great Depression. In Britain, the Financial Conduct Authority writes rules, po­lices fi­nance and in­ves­ti­gates, then takes its case to a tri­bunal.

The price is tol­er­a­ble only if Parliament del­e­gates nar­rowly, one mar­ket fail­ure at a time. An air­port reg­u­la­tor, Shah said, should reg­u­late the re­turn on a mo­nop­oly, not act as “feu­dal lord of air­ports”. {099-J06}
~ The reg­u­la­tor, he said, is Parliament’s agent for draft­ing law: “Please note, you’re not a feu­dal lord.”

quote.text: A civil ser­vant should never have the power to pun­ish you.

sections.label: Where it went wrong
sections.head: The three-headed regulator
sections.caption: how India fused all three powers
body: In India, Ajay Shah said, “very strange and re­mark­able things hap­pened”. Regulators such as RBI and SEBI com­bined[[x12]] the pow­ers to write reg­u­la­tions, in­ves­ti­gate, li­cense and pros­e­cute with the ju­di­cial power to pun­ish[[x13]].
He knows many of the peo­ple who laid their foun­da­tions, and calls them won­der­ful peo­ple who meant well. “But this is knowl­edge,” he said. “And they just did not have that knowl­edge.”
## A clue­less econ­o­mist

The first to see the prob­lem, Shah said, was Dr Sahu, who had worked in the Ministry of Finance, SEBI and the Competition Commission. In 2012 he wrote a paper and began giv­ing talks point­ing out that this vi­o­lated the sep­a­ra­tion of pow­ers. “For me it was just like wow, how did I not know this?” Shah said. “I was a clue­less econ­o­mist.” {099-S03}

Imagine, he said, that you are a bank or an air­port. Your reg­u­la­tor can deny you a li­cence and pun­ish you with­out due process or trans­parency. So you shut up, praise the reg­u­la­tor and lobby it to keep ri­vals out. {099-C12}
~ Asked by Amit Varma for a sum­mary, Shah listed the in­puts: sweep­ing law-making power, fused pow­ers and low rule of law. The out­come: lost dy­namism, in­no­va­tion, entry and com­pe­ti­tion.

quote.text: This is largely not true be­cause ac­tu­ally some­thing like 75% of the econ­omy came under the foot­print of reg­u­la­tors.

sections.label: The cure
sections.head: Rewrite the founding law
sections.caption: how to fix the regulators
body: The site of ac­tion, Ajay Shah said, is the law that cre­ates each reg­u­la­tor, and the fix comes in three parts.

First, nar­row the power to write law. Parliament can­not hand un­elected of­fi­cials unchecked power; each del­e­ga­tion should be a care­ful sec­tion with an ob­jec­tive and bal­anc­ing con­sid­er­a­tions.

Second, wrap rule-making and li­cens­ing in due process. Because reg­u­la­tors are not elected, they have a short­fall of demo­cratic le­git­i­macy. And re­fus­ing a li­cence, Shah said, is tan­ta­mount to harm­ing some­one, so the ag­grieved should be able to ap­peal.

Third, move the power to pun­ish out. Research at his or­gan­i­sa­tion, XKDR Forum[[x14]], on the Bombay and Delhi High Courts has changed his view. {#highcourts} Do it like the UK and Australia, he now says: let the reg­u­la­tor take its case to the High Court.
## A law for every agency

None of this is spe­cific to one reg­u­la­tor, Shah said. America has had a gen­eral law since 1946, the Administrative Procedures Act[[x15]], which ap­plies to all fed­eral agen­cies and came as a Republican push­back against Democrats cre­at­ing too many. “Don’t you envy these coun­tries?” {099-R14}
~ Court chal­lenges under it built a ju­rispru­dence that con­strains American reg­u­la­tors, and the courts, Shah said, are now “all over the work­ing of these reg­u­la­tory agen­cies”. {099-J15}

quote.text: It is not about SEBI, it is not about FSSAI, it is not about RERA, it’s ac­tu­ally a gen­eral tech­nol­ogy.

sections.label: Ideas people
sections.head: Lawyers code, thinkers design
sections.caption: the ecosystem of ideas people
body: Amit Varma asked two ques­tions. Does India still lack the philo­soph­i­cal foun­da­tions, the kind that left Ajay Shah, by his own ac­count, a clue­less econ­o­mist? And does it have the peo­ple to keep re­forms alive?

On the first, Shah said India’s doc­tor-engineer ob­ses­sion starved law, phi­los­o­phy, po­lit­i­cal sci­ence and pub­lic ad­min­is­tra­tion. {#doctorengineer} What hu­man­i­ties it has too often be­came a sim­plis­tic po­lit­i­cal project around so­cial jus­tice.

Indian law schools, he said, teach stu­dents to lit­i­gate around a sec­tion, not to de­sign one. That takes po­lit­i­cal phi­los­o­phy, pub­lic eco­nom­ics and his­tory. “You have to know about the rise of Nazi Germany to think about sur­veil­lance.” {#nazi}
## Twenty years ahead

Lawyers, Shah said, are the coders; the thinkers be­long up­stream[[x16]]. The fu­ture of India rides on re­search and re­form teams that stay en­gaged for years and keep five, ten or twenty years ahead of the of­fi­cials. Without one, the pen­sion re­form found no­body to de­fend it. {#pension}
~ His ad­vice to the young is blunt. Without mas­tery and ex­per­tise, he said, they have no busi­ness in pub­lic pol­icy: “please go work in a bank”. {#mastery}

quote.text: If you will work to the agenda of today’s joint sec­re­tary and today’s sec­re­tary, then that’s not progress.
If we had any philoso­phers worth their salt in India, they should be stand­ing up and say­ing, How dare you? You’re an un­elected of­fi­cial. How dare you have the power to write law?

p3.title: Tales of the regulators
p3.deck: A commission, a chairman, a bitter aide and a misread film

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the reform commission he helped to run
stories.head: The cathedral that was never built
body: In 2011, the fi­nance min­is­ter Pranab Mukherjee kicked off the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission[[x17]]. It was begun by KP Krishnan in the Department of Economic Affairs and chaired by Justice Srikrishna. {099-S05}

Ajay Shah’s part in it began with what he called “the only job in­ter­view of my en­tire life”, con­ducted by Justice Srikrishna. He went on to co-lead the commission’s tech­ni­cal team with Ila Patnaik.

The com­mis­sion drafted a clean, mod­ern law to re­place sixty bad fi­nan­cial laws. {#sixty} Its first part held about 140 sec­tions of gen­eral reg­u­la­tory the­ory: who sits on a regulator’s board, how the board votes, how the reg­u­la­tor leg­is­lates and in­ves­ti­gates. Its sec­ond part went through the fi­nan­cial sys­tem mar­ket fail­ure by mar­ket fail­ure, grant­ing one nar­row power at a time.
The first drafts took from 2011 to 2013. Then 800 pub­lic com­ments came in, and the same team pro­cessed them over two more years, fin­ish­ing in 2015. {#comments}

The law-drafting team, young grad­u­ates of India’s top law schools, was trained by one of the world’s top law drafters. Shah calls the re­sult the clean­est, best-drafted mod­ern law-drafting project in Indian his­tory.
Ten years on, the law has not been en­acted. “In a way, the project is a fail­ure,” Shah said. {#failure}

~ But ideas in­cu­bated in­side it, such as in­fla­tion tar­get­ing and a mon­e­tary pol­icy com­mit­tee that votes rather than leav­ing the in­ter­est rate to one gov­er­nor, later be­came a sep­a­rate law.
stories.why: Democracies do not progress through one grand project en­acted whole, Shah ar­gued. They progress by build­ing in­tel­lec­tual prod­ucts and per­suad­ing again and again, until ideas creep into prac­tice one by one. {099-C16}
stories.postscript: Varma, who had never heard the first vol­ume de­scribed this way, promised to read it.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the only job interview of his life

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a regulator who chose to be checked
stories.head: A chairman ties his own hands
body: The team that drafted the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code had im­ported the FSLRC’s 140 sec­tions on how a reg­u­la­tor should work. Inside the gov­ern­ment they were deleted, Ajay Shah said, and re­placed by “the bad 15 sec­tions from the SEBI Act”[[x18]]. {#fifteen}
So when Dr Sahu be­came the first chair­man of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board[[x19]] of India, the law im­posed no checks on him. He knew that with­out them, things would go badly.
He cre­ated checks him­self, split­ting IBBI into leg­isla­tive, ex­ec­u­tive and ju­di­cial de­part­ments. “So he did sep­a­ra­tion of pow­ers in­side the IBBI,” Shah said. {099-S04}
~ Then, around 2016 or 2017, the IBBI board en­acted a reg­u­la­tion gov­ern­ing how IBBI makes reg­u­la­tions, im­port­ing part of the FSLRC pro­ce­dure.
stories.why: When the law can­not be fixed, a re­former who holds power can still bind him­self. Shah likened it to the agree­ments be­tween the Finance Ministry and RBI that came be­fore a proper law.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Dr Sahu’s checks on himself

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on why Washington defeats its reformers
stories.head: Even the president’s man despaired
body: When the writer Jonathan Rauch first came to Washington in the mid-1980s, he chat­ted with David Stockman, Ronald Reagan’s man. Reagan’s rhetoric promised to make gov­ern­ment small and lean. {099-S07}

Stockman, Amit Varma said, was deeply de­pressed and bit­ter. They had come with such good in­ten­tions, and it was so dif­fi­cult to get any­thing done. “He is a president’s man,” Varma said. “Imagine it’s hard for the pres­i­dent to get any­thing done.”
Later, Rauch writes, the Democrat Bill Clinton and the Republican Newt Gingrich each tried, in dif­fer­ent ways, to do the same thing. Both failed mis­er­ably.

~ Rauch’s book, *Government’s End*, which Varma said blew his mind, has a word for the con­di­tion: de­moscle­ro­sis. Interest groups and reg­u­la­tions mul­ti­ply until they are al­most im­pos­si­ble to re­verse, and they crowd out other pol­i­cy­mak­ing. {099-C06}

quote.text: His point was what hap­pens is that the in­ter­est groups just mul­ti­ply, mul­ti­ply, mul­ti­ply, mul­ti­ply.

stories.postscript: A friend in DC told Varma a joke: throw a stone one way, you hit a legal firm; an­other, a lob­by­ing firm.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on David Stockman’s despair

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a film that misread prohibition
stories.head: The gangster who got it backwards
body: When the Shah Rukh Khan film *Raees*[[x20]] came out, Amit Varma wrote that it got basic eco­nom­ics wrong. {099-S08}
In the film, a politi­cian tours the town cam­paign­ing for pro­hi­bi­tion, and Shah Rukh Khan’s char­ac­ter, a boot­leg­ger, tries to stop him.

“And I’m like, wait a minute,” Varma said. “It is in the bootlegger’s in­ter­est to have pro­hi­bi­tion be­cause that is how his busi­ness flour­ishes.” A ban on drink­ing, he said, does not solve the prob­lem; it brings up an un­der­ground where boot­leg­gers make a lot of money.

~ This is the in­sight of Bruce Yandle[[x21]], the reg­u­la­tory econ­o­mist, whose essay Varma called “a beau­ti­ful way of think­ing about how reg­u­la­tion works”. The moral cru­sader and the prof­i­teer are nat­u­ral al­lies, and some­times the boot­leg­ger funds the Baptist. {099-C07}
stories.why: A cam­paign for a ban often has two spon­sors: the moral­ist who wants it on prin­ci­ple and the prof­i­teer who needs it to stay in busi­ness. Varma’s first ques­tion for any reg­u­la­tion ap­plies: who does this ben­e­fit? {099-C02}

quiz.q: How much of the economy, by Ajay Shah’s estimate, came under regulators after 1991?
quiz.a: Something like 75 per cent, under more in­tru­sive cen­tral plan­ning than ever be­fore.

quiz.q: Which three Indian regulators now have regulations governing how they make regulations?
quiz.a: IBBI first, then SEBI, and RBI on the morn­ing of record­ing.

quiz.q: Who conducted what Ajay Shah called the only job interview of his entire life?
quiz.a: Justice Srikrishna, the chair­man of the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission.

quiz.q: What three questions does Amit Varma ask of any regulation?
quiz.a: Who does this ben­e­fit, who does it hurt, and what are the un­in­tended con­se­quences?

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 99. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Friedrich Hayek (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); Jonathan Rauch (New America, CC BY 2.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Regulation: A Primer
shelf.creator: Susan Dudley and Jerry Brito
shelf.why: Amit calls it a won­der­ful book.

shelf.title: Government’s End: Why Washington Stopped Working
shelf.creator: Jonathan Rauch
shelf.why: Rauch’s ac­count of how spe­cial in­ter­ests cap­tured the American state, coin­ing ‘demosclerosis’: in­ter­est groups and reg­u­la­tions mul­ti­ply until they are nearly im­pos­si­ble to re­verse and crowd out other pol­i­cy­mak­ing.

shelf.title: The Theory of Economic Regulation
shelf.creator: George Stigler
shelf.why: A fa­mous 1971 essay with three ax­ioms.

shelf.title: Bootleggers and Baptists: The Education of a Regulatory Economist
shelf.creator: Bruce Yandle
shelf.why: Yandle’s ‘beau­ti­ful way of think­ing about how reg­u­la­tion works’: the moral cru­sader (the Baptist) and the black-market sup­plier (the boot­leg­ger) both want the ban, so they lobby for the same end, some­times with the boot­leg­ger fund­ing the Baptist.

shelf.title: Fortress and Frontier in American Health Care
shelf.creator: Robert Graboyes
shelf.why: It gave Amit ‘a new frame­work to think about the world’.

shelf.title: Raees: An Empty Shell of a Gangster Film
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s re­view ar­gu­ing that the film gets pro­hi­bi­tion eco­nom­ics back­wards: a real boot­leg­ger would fund the anti-alcohol politi­cian, not fight him, be­cause their in­cen­tives are aligned.

shelf.title: The Baptist, the Bootlegger and the Dead Man Walking
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ten ac­count of the Lal Bihari saga, which ap­plies the boot­leg­gers-and-Baptists frame­work.

shelf.title: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission (FSLRC) Report, Volume 1
shelf.creator: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission
shelf.why: The FSLRC re­port, a crisp sum­mary of 20 years of Indian re­search on reg­u­la­tion writ­ten as com­pact chap­ters end­ing in draft­ing in­struc­tions, and the draft Indian Financial Code it pro­duced.

shelf.title: FSLRC Volume 2: The Indian Financial Code (draft law)
shelf.creator: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission
shelf.why: The FSLRC re­port, a crisp sum­mary of 20 years of Indian re­search on reg­u­la­tion writ­ten as com­pact chap­ters end­ing in draft­ing in­struc­tions, and the draft Indian Financial Code it pro­duced.

shelf.title: The LEAP Blog
shelf.why: The peer-reviewed re­search blog Ajay co-edits, where his ideas are avail­able to any­one at any time.

shelf.title: Making Regulation in India Work Better
shelf.creator: KP Krishnan
shelf.why: A talk on fix­ing Indian reg­u­la­tion by the of­fi­cial who started the FSLRC project.

shelf.title: Rethinking Regulation in India (talk and slides)
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A fuller pre­sen­ta­tion of the reg­u­la­tory-theory ar­gu­ment Ajay makes in this episode.

shelf.title: A Deregulatory Moment
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s writ­ten take on the cur­rent open­ing for re­form­ing India’s reg­u­la­tory state.

shelf.title: The Administrative Procedures Act (1946)
shelf.why: The 1946 US law that binds every fed­eral agency to a sin­gle rule­book, which Ajay calls a bril­liant blue­print for checks and bal­ances on reg­u­la­tors and the same idea as India’s draft Indian Financial Code.

shelf.title: Understanding the State (Episode 25)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on mar­ket fail­ure in its pre­cise tech­ni­cal sense (pub­lic goods, ex­ter­nal­i­ties and the rest) and on the nar­row con­di­tions under which the state may in­ter­vene, con­di­tions that are nec­es­sary but not suf­fi­cient.

shelf.title: Don’t Punish Victimless Crimes (Episode 73)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It cov­ers why ban­ning drink­ing doesn’t solve the prob­lem but cre­ates an un­der­ground run by boot­leg­gers.

shelf.title: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s ac­count of re­vers­ing his di­a­betes through diet: eat less ce­real, avoid pro­cessed food, and treat ghee as a su­per­food and sugar as poi­son.

shelf.title: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Explains that politi­cians and bu­reau­crats re­spond to in­cen­tives like ev­ery­one else, so the state is no benev­o­lent beast and gov­ern­ment fail­ure is far more com­mon than mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: Rethinking Innovation Policy (Episode 59)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why re­search fund­ing in India is ‘a truly bad space’, and the al­ter­na­tive: an in­dus­try-neutral ap­proach that con­tracts R&D out through grants to uni­ver­si­ties and pri­vate firms rather than hav­ing bu­reau­crats pick sec­tors.

shelf.title: Separation of Powers (Episode 91)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why fus­ing leg­isla­tive, ex­ec­u­tive and ju­di­cial pow­ers, as Indian reg­u­la­tors do, is so dan­ger­ous.

shelf.title: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ the­ory of change: pol­icy im­proves through a decades-long pipe­line of data, re­search, rival pro­pos­als, pub­lic de­bate, com­mit­tee re­ports and draft laws, not by whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear.

shelf.title: Inflation Targeting Rocks! (Episode 68)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The full story of in­fla­tion tar­get­ing, which Ajay pushed for from the 1990s and which took more than fif­teen years to be­come law: a les­son in how slowly good pol­icy ar­rives.

shelf.title: Going Bankrupt in India (Episode 80)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why bank­ruptcy is a healthy, nor­mal part of eco­nomic life, and how the pol­i­tics of India’s bank­ruptcy re­form gave big com­pa­nies out­sized in­flu­ence, left op­er­a­tional cred­i­tors weak and squeezed small manufacturers’ work­ing cap­i­tal.

shelf.title: The Globalisation Episode and Is Globalisation Doomed? (Episodes 95 and 96 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ foun­da­tional think­ing on glob­al­i­sa­tion: first prin­ci­ples, a pot­ted in­tel­lec­tual his­tory up to the Second World War, and why tar­iffs harm a country’s own peo­ple and shift wealth from the poor to the rich.

shelf.title: India’s Massive Pensions Crisis (Episode 347 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Ajay and Renuka Sane on the old ver­sus new pen­sion scheme: a bi­par­ti­san re­form built by a small in­tel­lec­tual com­mu­nity, and how in­sti­tu­tional mem­ory van­ished once that com­mu­nity dis­persed.

laughs.text: Amit’s open­ing: ‘we have two pieces of good news for you, which are that I’m Amit and he’s Ajay. No no no. We have two ac­tual pieces of good news for you.’
Amit’s block­buster pitch for the India-UK FTA, ‘Return to Zero’: ‘India in­vented zero, and now these tar­iffs are gonna go back to zero now. Now the for­eign­ers are bring­ing zero back to India.’

Amit nee­dles Ajay that decades of econ­o­mists couldn’t lib­er­alise trade: ‘Who got it done? Donald Trump got it done.’ Ajay: ‘Amitbhai, you and I should nom­i­nate Donald Trump for the Bharat Ratna.’ Amit, hastily: ‘He is jok­ing... peo­ple are gonna like clip this and put this on Twitter and say he’s a Trump bhakt.’

After Ajay’s care­ful def­i­ni­tions, Amit says: ‘I love the way you say reg­u­la­tion and reg­u­la­tor. I could lis­ten to you all day.’ Ajay apol­o­gises: ‘for­give me, this is a life­time of angst.’
A joke from Amit’s friend about Washington DC: throw a stone in one di­rec­tion and you’ll hit a legal firm, throw it in an­other and you’ll hit a lob­by­ing firm.
Ajay on what sur­gi­cal del­e­ga­tion should pre­vent: a reg­u­la­tor act­ing as ‘feu­dal lord of airports’, de­cid­ing ‘what shall be the color of the mir­rors in the loo’.
Amit’s hum­ble­brag while rec­om­mend­ing Graboyes: he won the Bastiat Prize in 2014, ‘the year be­fore I won it for the sec­ond time.’
Amit to Ajay: ‘You were a clue­less econ­o­mist in your words. I’m not call­ing you names.’
Amit on in­cre­men­tal re­form: ‘One baby step at a time, the in­fant crawls away from the precipice, but it can still hear the la­bored breath­ing of the mon­ster.’
Amit, after hear­ing about the 25-year jour­ney, on the show’s own prospects: ‘twenty-three years later Everything is Everything will have its first viral video. That is my hope.’
Behind-the-scenes clip on rec­om­men­da­tions per­pet­u­ally de­ferred to ‘next episode’: ‘Every episode he does this. The sev­ens are mul­ti­ply­ing. Compound in­ter­est.’
Amit on his book pick: ‘this episode is ac­tu­ally the rec­om­men­da­tion. So please watch this episode, but if you are watch­ing this, you al­ready have. So please watch it again.’
Amit reaches for the clas­sic maxim after Ajay’s ac­count of regulators’ fused pow­ers: ‘power cor­rupts, ab­so­lute power cor­rupts ab­so­lutely.’

Recent US de­vel­op­ments re­called from the Separation of Powers episode: the right to a jury trial being used to knock out tri­als run in­side the SEC, and de­vel­op­ments around Chevron Doctrine. Courts are now ‘all over the work­ing of these reg­u­la­tory agencies’.
Amit asks whether an econ­o­mist re­ally needs 17th-century po­lit­i­cal phi­los­o­phy and even the Magna Carta, and an­swers ‘frankly, yes’: depth isn’t enough with­out breadth.
